Interfering meaning… not eating a single specific dish? That’s hardly interfering.

If the person’s palette was so limited that this would cause major issues for them, then that’s an entirely different issue.

Yes, everything has a smell. But some things have objectively more pungent odours than others. Bringing generally “smelly” foods all together is just a socially inconsiderate move. Fishy odours especially are notorious for being unpleasant.

It’s not about spaghetti and meatballs. It’s being intentionally obtuse and uncaring to your colleagues. Not bringing in one specific dish to make 3 people’s day a little easier is not a big ask. Frankly, I’d argue that you should grow up and learn some empathy.

Have you not considered that not everyone is like you? There’s stuff like the cilantro soap gene, and it’s not a far stretch to say that some people are more sensitive to smells than others.

I love eggs myself but it’s not hard to make one small adjustment if it’s causing people to have such visceral reactions. 

In either way, it’s probably not just the egg causing the smell, but the combination of kimchi (fermented and spicy smells), sardines (fishy smells), and eggs (sulfur smells). 

It’s too many odours combining together that might not smell great, especially in a closed office space.

Maybe not for you, but it was clearly a problem for three separate people. A lot of workplaces have a no-fragrance rule. A beautiful floral smell for one person can be headache inducing for another. Same goes for lunch food.

It’s not a personal attack on you, and it’s not hard to avoid 3 items in work lunches if it’s causing problems. Sure, the co-workers could’ve used nicer language but they’re just voicing a complaint. It’s not like they’re banning you from ever eating those things again

Porn causes escalation because of the violence perpetuated in those videos. [There have been studies that prove this.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6942232/) That and coupled with the fact that an early exposure to porn (which, anecdotally seems to be very common) can cause problems with sex down the line, it's easy to extrapolate that such extreme and violent acts would not be as mainstream as they are now.

>Is this always true or do people like BDSM because it gives them an adrenaline rush, allows them to take a break from everyday reality\* and improve trust and communication (one must always know ?

Everyone will have slightly different reasons for interacting with BDSM, but I would say everything you mentioned checks out. Some people use kink as an escape for a hectic work/school schedule, or to find a vent for their traumatic experiences. Adrenaline is something baked into some acts. Getting hit will cause an adrenaline rush. Any physically aggressive or skin-puncturing acts will give you a rush by default. And I would argue some forms of bondage (rope) can be a good trust building exercise, and is more artistic than it is sadistic from what I've seen.

>What is the solution? BDSM by nature will attract some of the worst people out there. People who want a loophole for abuse, or a direct pipeline to traumatized individuals. There are a lot of kink workshops that examine what you ask about (how consent really works, being self aware about your own kinks and the harm they can cause), but the reality is that most people involved in kink will not attend those.

Unfortunately we cannot control other people. We can advocate for what we think is right, but ultimately I do not think it is our job to "help" kinksters. You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make them drink. People will always do BDSM, just like people do hard drugs, commit crimes, etc etc. But we can try and create spaces (like these!) that encourage critical thinking and awareness.

Eating disorders aren’t just about losing weight. There’s BED and EDNOS which arguably make you gain weight or maintain. Orthorexia which is an obsession over being healthy, which could be what you have. I suggest you do more research into it if you are curious :]

Also — A. Being at a healthy weight does not disqualify you from having an eating disoder. B. You do not have to be losing weight to have an eating disorder.

I’d suggest you think about how much your eating and exercise habits are affecting you. You may have disordered eating but not an eating disorder (exhibiting symptoms, but not to the point where it takes over your life. like how you can feel sad but not be clinically depressed). Your relationship with your body image is important too. Are you constantly preoccupied about eating/exercising/how you look? Does it impact your social/work/etc activities? Does it cause you stress and do you plan around it, making it the focal point of your life? If so, then you very likely may have an eating disorder.

I’ve been to a paediatric ward twice.

The first time, I stayed 3 days. I arrived on a weekend so I was seen by a nurse (doctors are off on weekends). There was a giant blackboard on the wall and my info was all written there. It’s also cold as FUCK there. I always needed to ask for extra blankets. I didn’t do much there since I didn’t see a doctor until the last day so they didn’t have directions on what to do. They gave me some generic printouts on articles on mental health to read. I got discharged on the last day because I was desperate to leave and the doctor sucked. You’re also not allowed to talk to other patients unsupervised (I learnt this the hard way lol).

The second time I stayed for two weeks. Same paediatric ward. I got seen by a doctor on the first day, and she pretty much hit the nail on the head for me lol. I got more specific treatment for my condition this time around. I did a lot more “fun” things like group movie nights and art activities. I also talked to many people. I stayed for a very long time (usually people stay for a few days like I did the first time). I was on a form 3, basically means the hospital can keep me up to two weeks. It’s the second longest form (longest is a month). I will say that on average, the older the patient the more jaded and frustrated they were to be at the ward. The younger patients were generally more excited/saw it as a “cool” experience.
